questions.q: Inside the HIV capsid, the viral enzyme protease is needed to:
o: Cut large viral polyproteins into functional proteins so new virions mature
Copy the viral RNA into DNA
Insert viral DNA into the host chromosome
Attach the virus to the CD4 receptor
questions.x: Protease cleaves long viral polyproteins into working capsid proteins and enzymes, letting new particles mature. Copying RNA into DNA is the job of reverse transcriptase, and insertion is done by integrase.

questions.q: Which combination of features correctly describes HIV?
o: Enveloped virus with single-stranded DNA and no enzymes
Enveloped virus with RNA and the enzyme reverse transcriptase
Naked virus with RNA and a protein tail
questions.x: HIV has a lipid envelope with glycoprotein spikes, an RNA genome and carries reverse transcriptase, which makes it a retrovirus.

questions.q: Which pairing of a stage of respiration with its site in a eukaryotic cell is NOT correct?
questions.x: The electron carriers sit in the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae), not the matrix. The other three pairings are correct.

questions.q: During long, hard exercise, the build-up of lactic acid in skeletal muscles is linked with:
o: Release of urea from the muscle
questions.x: When oxygen is short, muscles make lactic acid by fermentation. Its build-up lowers the pH in the muscle and is linked with muscle fatigue; it does not raise ATP output or release urea.

questions.q: Phosphodiester bonds are the linkages that join the monomers of:
questions.x: In DNA and RNA, the nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next. Polysaccharides use glycosidic bonds, proteins peptide bonds and triglycerides ester bonds.

questions.q: Which mineral element is part of bones and teeth, together with calcium, and is also part of ATP?
questions.x: Bones and teeth contain calcium phosphate, and ATP contains phosphate groups. Iron is part of haemoglobin, iodine of thyroxine and magnesium of chlorophyll.

questions.q: A single RNA strand of 300 nucleotides contains how many ribose molecules?
questions.x: Each RNA nucleotide has one ribose, one phosphate and one base, so 300 nucleotides contain 300 ribose molecules. Being single-stranded, there is no second strand to double the count.

questions.q: On a tRNA molecule, the anticodon is located:
o: At the 3′ end, next to the CCA sequence
At the 5′ end, joined to the amino acid
On a loop at the opposite end from the amino acid attachment site
In the stem that carries the amino acid
questions.x: The amino acid attaches at the 3′ CCA end, while the anticodon lies on a loop at the far end of the cloverleaf, where it can pair with the mRNA codon.

questions.q: A polar molecule is one that:
o: Contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms
Has the same charge spread evenly over all its atoms
Has an uneven distribution of charge, with a partly positive end and a partly negative end
questions.x: In a polar molecule such as water, electrons are shared unequally, giving partial positive and negative ends. Molecules of only carbon and hydrogen are usually non-polar.

questions.q: A fatty acid is described as saturated when:
o: Its chain contains at least one C=C double bond
All the carbon–carbon bonds in its chain are single bonds
It is joined to glycerol by an ester bond
questions.x: A saturated fatty acid carries the maximum number of hydrogen atoms, so every C–C bond is single. A chain with one or more C=C double bonds is unsaturated.

questions.q: Which of the following is a macromolecule?
questions.x: Glycogen is a large polysaccharide made of thousands of glucose units. Sucrose (a disaccharide), glycerol and alanine (an amino acid) are small micromolecules.

questions.q: The pH of pure water at 25 °C is:
questions.x: Pure water ionizes slightly into equal amounts of H⁺ and OH⁻ (each 10⁻⁷ mol/L), so its pH is 7, which is neutral.

questions.q: A human insulin gene placed in bacteria makes them produce human insulin. This is possible mainly because the genetic code is:
questions.x: Almost all organisms use the same codons for the same amino acids, so bacteria read the human gene correctly. The code is not overlapping or ambiguous.

questions.q: A DNA molecule is 68 nm long. Using the Watson–Crick dimensions, how many complete turns does its double helix make?
questions.x: One complete turn is 3.4 nm long, so 68 ÷ 3.4 = 20 turns. 200 is the number of base pairs (68 ÷ 0.34), not turns.

questions.q: Glycerol and fatty acids combine to form a fat by a reaction called:
o: Hydrolysis, in which water is added
Condensation, in which water is removed
Oxidation, in which hydrogen is removed
Neutralisation, in which a salt is formed
questions.x: Each ester bond forms by condensation (dehydration synthesis), removing one water molecule. Hydrolysis is the reverse reaction that breaks the fat down.

questions.q: A DNA segment of 60 base pairs is held together by 140 hydrogen bonds. How many of its base pairs are guanine–cytosine pairs?
questions.x: If all 60 pairs were A–T there would be 120 hydrogen bonds. Each G–C pair adds one extra bond, so 140 − 120 = 20 pairs are G–C (and 40 are A–T).

questions.q: When a green tomato ripens and turns red, its plastids change from:
questions.x: During ripening chlorophyll breaks down and the chloroplasts become chromoplasts rich in red carotenoids such as lycopene.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the DNA of a eukaryotic nucleus with that of a bacterium?
o: Eukaryotic DNA is a single circular molecule without proteins
Eukaryotic DNA is linear, divided into several chromosomes and bound to histones
Bacterial DNA is enclosed in a nuclear envelope
Bacterial DNA is divided into many linear chromosomes
questions.x: Eukaryotic nuclei hold several linear chromosomes in which DNA is packed with histones. A bacterium has one circular DNA molecule lying free in the nucleoid.

questions.q: The mitochondria of a sperm cell are packed in its:
questions.x: The middle piece is packed with mitochondria that supply ATP for the beating of the tail.

questions.q: Which pairing of an ER type with a main product is correct?
o: Smooth ER – lipids such as phospholipids and steroids
questions.x: Smooth ER makes lipids, including membrane phospholipids and steroids. Rough ER, with its ribosomes, makes proteins such as secretory enzymes.

questions.q: Which structure lies directly above the hypothalamus in the forebrain?
questions.x: The thalamus lies just above the hypothalamus; both form the diencephalon. The pons, cerebellum and medulla are hindbrain parts lying lower down.

questions.q: When the layers of a Pacinian corpuscle are squeezed by firm pressure, the corpuscle transduces:
questions.x: Pressure is mechanical energy; deforming the corpuscle sets up impulses in its nerve ending. That is why it is classed as a mechanoreceptor.

questions.q: Compared with motor neurons, associative (relay) neurons usually have:
o: Very long axons that reach muscles
Cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia
Thick myelin sheaths made by Schwann cells
Short axons and link neurons inside the CNS
questions.x: Associative neurons are short and connect sensory and motor neurons within the brain and spinal cord. Long axons reaching muscles belong to motor neurons.

questions.q: Sneezing when dust irritates the lining of the nose is a reflex whose centre lies in the brainstem. It is classified as a:
questions.x: Reflexes integrated in the brain (here the brainstem) and using cranial nerves are cranial reflexes. Sneezing is inborn, so it is not a conditioned reflex, and it happens without a conscious decision.

questions.q: The highly branched dendrites of a motor neuron are an advantage because they:
o: Provide a large surface to receive signals from many other neurons
Insulate the cell body from ions
Store the ATP the neuron needs
questions.x: Branching gives a large area for synapses with many other neurons. Releasing transmitter onto muscle is done by the axon terminals.

questions.q: Which part of the brain is the main control centre of the autonomic nervous system?
questions.x: The hypothalamus controls the autonomic nervous system and so regulates involuntary activities of internal organs. The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement and the corpus callosum links the hemispheres.

questions.q: Receptors in muscles, tendons and joints that keep the brain informed about the position of body parts are called:
questions.x: Proprioceptors, such as muscle spindles, signal the position and stretch of muscles and joints. Nociceptors detect pain and osmoreceptors detect blood concentration.

questions.q: When a stimulus acts on a receptor, the first change that leads to nerve impulses is:
o: Release of neurotransmitter from the receptor into the blood
A rise in ATP production by the receptor's mitochondria
A change in the permeability of the receptor membrane to ions
questions.x: Transduction begins when the stimulus alters ion permeability of the receptor membrane, producing a generator potential. If this reaches threshold, impulses follow.

questions.q: Carbonic anhydrase speeds up the formation of carbonic acid from carbon dioxide and water in the tissues, and its breakdown in the lungs. This shows that an enzyme:
o: Can work in one direction only
Changes the products of the reaction
Is used up in the lungs
Can catalyse a reversible reaction in either direction
questions.x: An enzyme speeds up both directions of a reversible reaction; the direction taken depends on the concentrations of reactants and products.

questions.q: The names of most enzymes are formed by adding which suffix to the name of the substrate or reaction?
questions.x: Most enzymes are named by adding '-ase', as in maltase (acts on maltose) and lipase (acts on lipids). The ending '-ose' is used for sugars.

questions.q: In an experiment, samples of a starch and amylase mixture are tested with iodine at intervals. The end point of digestion is reached when iodine:
o: No longer turns blue-black, showing the starch is used up
questions.x: Iodine turns blue-black with starch. When all the starch has been digested, the sample stays yellow-brown, the colour of the iodine itself.

questions.q: Enzymes in living cells catalyse:
questions.x: Enzymes control all of metabolism, from synthesis of proteins and DNA to the breakdown of food and respiratory substrates.

questions.q: Heavy metal ions such as mercury (Hg²⁺) and lead (Pb²⁺) inhibit enzymes mainly by:
o: Binding to sulphur-containing (–SH) groups and changing the enzyme's shape
Raising the pH of the cell
questions.x: These metal ions combine with –SH groups of the enzyme's amino acids, distorting its shape. This is why they are poisonous.

questions.q: Which statement gives a Lamarckian, NOT a Darwinian, explanation?
o: Snakes lost their legs because they stopped using them while crawling
Moths matching the bark colour were eaten less and left more offspring
Insects already resistant to a pesticide survived and multiplied
Finches with beaks suited to local seeds left more young
questions.x: Loss of an organ through disuse, followed by inheritance of the loss, is Lamarck's idea. The other three describe selection acting on variation that already existed.

questions.q: The idea that the first living organisms took ready-made organic food from their surroundings is called the:
questions.x: The heterotroph hypothesis says the first cells fed on the organic molecules of the primitive soup. Autotrophs that make their own food evolved later.

questions.q: As the first heterotrophs multiplied, the organic molecules in the early seas were gradually used up. Which organisms would then have had the greatest advantage?
o: Cells that could only absorb ready-made amino acids
Cells that needed free oxygen to respire
Cells that had lost their ability to divide
Cells that could make their own food from simple inorganic substances
questions.x: Once the soup ran low, cells that could make organic food themselves, such as early photosynthetic prokaryotes, could survive and spread. Oxygen was not yet available for aerobic cells.

questions.q: Symptoms of gonorrhoea in an infected man usually appear:
o: Within about a week of infection
Only after the person reaches old age
questions.x: Gonorrhoea has a short incubation period; symptoms such as painful urination and discharge usually appear within a few days to a week.

questions.q: The full form of AIDS is:
questions.x: AIDS stands for Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome, the late stage of infection with HIV, the human immunodeficiency virus.

questions.q: Which of the following helps to prevent the spread of HIV in hospitals and clinics?
o: Using sterile, disposable syringes and screened blood
questions.x: HIV is carried in blood, so single-use sterile syringes and screening of blood for transfusion stop its spread. Antibiotics do not act on viruses.

questions.q: The luteal phase lasts about 14 days in most women. A woman has regular 32-day cycles. Ovulation is expected on about:
questions.x: Ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next period: 32 − 14 = 18. The follicular phase varies, so day 14 applies only to 28-day cycles.

questions.q: Which hormone raises the blood calcium level by stimulating osteoclasts to release calcium from bone?
questions.x: Parathormone from the parathyroid glands increases bone resorption, releasing calcium into the blood. Calcitonin has the opposite effect.

questions.q: The clavicle is commonly known as the:
questions.x: The clavicle is the collar bone. The shoulder blade is the scapula, the breastbone is the sternum and the kneecap is the patella.

questions.q: The sarcoplasmic reticulum of a muscle fibre is a specialised form of the:
questions.x: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a modified smooth endoplasmic reticulum, a network of membrane sacs and tubes around each myofibril. It carries no ribosomes and is not part of the Golgi apparatus.

questions.q: The most common form of arthritis is:
questions.x: Osteoarthritis, linked to wear of joint cartilage with age, is by far the most common form. Rheumatoid arthritis, gout and infective arthritis are less common.

questions.q: Which description fits cardiac muscle but not skeletal muscle?
o: Branched cells joined end to end by intercalated discs
questions.x: Branching and intercalated discs are unique to cardiac muscle. Striations, sarcomeres and plentiful mitochondria are present in skeletal muscle as well.

questions.q: Which pair of features would be seen in the muscle of the small intestine wall but NOT in the biceps?
questions.x: The intestinal wall is smooth muscle: spindle-shaped, unstriated cells. Striations, many peripheral nuclei and sarcomeres belong to the biceps; intercalated discs are found only in the heart.

questions.q: Within a thin filament, troponin molecules are found:
o: Only at the M line in the centre of the sarcomere
On the heads of the myosin molecules
Free in the sarcoplasm between myofibrils
Attached to tropomyosin at regular intervals along the filament
questions.x: Troponin is a small protein complex bound to tropomyosin at regular intervals along the thin filament. It is part of the thin filament, not of myosin, and it is not free in the sarcoplasm.

questions.q: The length of the A band of a sarcomere is always equal to the length of:
o: Two thin filaments placed end to end
The I band plus the H zone
questions.x: The A band is defined by the thick filaments, so its length equals the length of a thick filament. That is why the A band stays the same length whether the sarcomere is relaxed or contracted.

questions.q: Genes A and B are 30 map units apart. A dihybrid with the arrangement Ab/aB is expected to form what percentage of AB gametes?
questions.x: With repulsion (Ab/aB), AB and ab are the recombinant gametes. Total recombinants are 30%, shared equally, so AB = 15%. Ab and aB are 35% each.

questions.q: Linkage between two genes is said to be complete when:
o: Crossing over occurs in every meiotic cell
The two genes lie on different chromosomes
Recombinants make up exactly half of the offspring
No crossing over occurs between them, so only parental types appear
questions.x: In complete linkage the genes are never separated, so the dihybrid gives only parental combinations. Recombinants at 50% would mean the genes behave as unlinked.

questions.q: The F1 of a monohybrid cross (Tt) is self-pollinated. What fraction of the F2 plants will breed true when they are themselves self-pollinated?
questions.x: Only homozygous plants breed true. In the F2, TT (1/4) and tt (1/4) together make 1/2. The Tt plants (1/2) segregate again.

questions.q: Genes X, Y and Z lie on one chromosome. Map distances are X–Y 20 units, Y–Z 15 units and X–Z 5 units. Which gene lies in the middle?
o: The order cannot be worked out from these data
questions.x: The largest distance (X–Y, 20) must be between the two outer genes. X–Z (5) + Z–Y (15) = 20, so the order is X–Z–Y and Z is in the middle.

questions.q: The phenotype of an organism is the result of:
o: Its genotype alone, unaffected by its surroundings
Its genotype acting together with the environment
The number of its chromosomes only
questions.x: Genes set the potential, and the environment influences how it is expressed, so phenotype = genotype + environment. Neither the genotype alone nor the environment alone fully decides it.

questions.q: In the cross AaBbCc × aabbcc, with independent genes and complete dominance, what fraction of the offspring shows the dominant phenotype for all three traits?
questions.x: For each gene, Aa × aa gives 1/2 dominant offspring. For all three: 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8. 27/64 would be the answer for AaBbCc × AaBbCc.

questions.q: Map units (centimorgans) on a linkage map measure:
o: The exact physical length of DNA in nanometres
The number of genes between two loci
Relative distance worked out from recombination frequency
The time taken for crossing over
questions.x: A map unit equals 1% recombination. It gives the relative distance between genes based on how often they are separated by crossing over, not a physical length.

questions.q: Mendel referred to the hereditary units that control characters as:
questions.x: Mendel called them 'factors'. The word 'gene' was introduced later (by Johannsen, 1909), and chromosomes were not linked to heredity in Mendel's time.

questions.q: Atherosclerosis is a condition in which:
o: Fatty deposits containing cholesterol build up in artery walls and narrow the lumen
Calcium salts make vein walls brittle
Valves of the veins stop working
The heart muscle becomes inflamed by infection
questions.x: In atherosclerosis, cholesterol-rich plaques form inside arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow. Hardening by calcium is described as arteriosclerosis.

questions.q: After the spleen is removed because of injury, a person can live normally but is more likely to:
questions.x: The spleen filters blood and helps fight blood-borne bacteria, so without it some infections become more likely. Bone marrow, the thymus and fat digestion are not affected.

questions.q: Narrowing of arteries by fatty deposits tends to raise blood pressure because:
o: The heart must pump harder to push blood through the narrower vessels
The narrowed arteries pump blood themselves
More plasma leaks into the tissues
The veins become wider and hold more blood
questions.x: A narrower lumen offers more resistance to blood flow, so the heart has to produce a higher pressure to move the same volume of blood.

questions.q: In a heartbeat of 0.8 second, the atrial muscle contracts for only 0.1 second. The atria therefore rest for:
questions.x: Rest time = 0.8 − 0.1 = 0.7 second. The value 0.5 second is the ventricles' rest time, since ventricular systole lasts 0.3 second.

questions.q: An attenuated vaccine contains pathogens that are:
o: Alive but weakened so that they do not cause the disease
Dead and broken into small pieces
questions.x: Attenuated means weakened. The live organisms can still stimulate the immune system but cannot cause the illness in healthy people.

questions.q: While T cells mature in the thymus, those that react strongly against the body's own antigens are:
o: Released into the blood as cytotoxic T cells
Destroyed, so the mature T cells tolerate self
questions.x: Self-reactive T cells are removed during maturation. This self-tolerance stops the immune system from attacking the body's own tissues.

questions.q: Which change in the blood is detected by the carotid and aortic bodies but NOT by the central chemoreceptors of the medulla?
o: A large fall in the oxygen level
A rise in the carbon dioxide level
A rise in the hydrogen ion concentration
A fall in the pH of cerebrospinal fluid
questions.x: The central chemoreceptors respond to carbon dioxide through the H⁺ it forms; they are not sensitive to oxygen. A marked fall in blood oxygen is sensed by the peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies.

questions.q: In a healthy person at rest, the haemoglobin in arterial blood leaving the lungs is about:
questions.x: At the alveolar pO₂ of about 100 mm Hg, haemoglobin becomes almost fully (about 97%) saturated. Mixed venous blood at rest is still about 75% saturated.

questions.q: The rate at which oxygen diffuses across the alveolar wall into the blood would INCREASE if:
o: The total surface area of the alveoli became smaller
Blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries stopped
The difference in oxygen partial pressure across the wall became larger
questions.x: Diffusion is faster with a larger concentration (partial pressure) gradient, a larger surface area and a thinner barrier. A thicker wall, a smaller area or stopped blood flow would all slow it.

questions.q: A smoker with chronic obstructive lung disease blows as hard as possible into a peak-flow meter. Compared with a healthy person, the reading will be:
o: Higher, because the lungs are larger
Higher, because extra mucus pushes the air out faster
The same, because peak flow does not depend on the airways
Lower, because the narrowed airways and weak recoil slow the outflow of air
questions.x: Peak flow measures how fast air can be blown out. Narrowed, mucus-filled bronchi and loss of elastic recoil in COPD slow expiration, so the peak-flow reading falls.

questions.q: After drinking milk, an adult regularly gets bloating and diarrhoea, but has no problem eating bread or table sugar. The most likely cause is:
o: Too little sucrase in the small intestine
Too little lactase in the small intestine
Too much hydrochloric acid in the stomach
questions.x: Milk sugar is lactose. Without enough lactase it stays undigested in the gut, where bacteria ferment it and cause gas and diarrhoea. Normal tolerance of bread (starch) and table sugar (sucrose) shows that amylase and sucrase are working.

questions.q: Intestinal juice is produced mainly by tubular glands that open between the bases of the villi. These glands are the:
questions.x: The crypts of Lieberkühn are pits between the villi whose cells secrete intestinal juice. Gastric glands are in the stomach, the islets are endocrine tissue in the pancreas, and the parotids are salivary glands.

questions.q: When blood pressure or blood volume falls, the kidneys release an enzyme that leads, through angiotensin, to aldosterone secretion. This enzyme is:
questions.x: Renin from the kidney starts the formation of angiotensin, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone. Rennin, spelt with two n's, is the milk-curdling enzyme of the infant stomach.

questions.q: Many patients with chronic kidney failure become anaemic. This is mainly because the damaged kidneys:
o: Make less erythropoietin, the hormone that stimulates red blood cell production
Filter red blood cells out into the urine
Produce too much urea, which bursts red cells
Store iron instead of releasing it
questions.x: The kidneys release erythropoietin, which stimulates the bone marrow to make red cells. Less of it means fewer red cells. Healthy or damaged glomeruli do not normally filter whole cells.

questions.q: Creatinine, a waste in urine, is removed from the blood by:
o: The lungs rather than the kidneys
questions.x: Creatinine is filtered at the glomerulus, and some extra is secreted into the tubule; little or none is reabsorbed. Complete reabsorption is the fate of glucose, not of a waste.

questions.q: A climber's fingers become pale and cold in freezing wind, while his core temperature stays near 37 °C. This shows that:
o: Skin arterioles constrict, keeping warm blood in the core at the cost of the extremities
His temperature set point has fallen
His fingers produce more heat than his core
questions.x: Vasoconstriction diverts blood away from the skin, which is why the fingers look pale and cool, but it protects the temperature of the vital organs.

questions.q: Spiders excrete much of their nitrogenous waste as:
questions.x: Guanine, a purine, is the main nitrogenous waste of spiders. Like uric acid it is insoluble, which saves water on land.

questions.q: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) means:
o: The volume of urine passed per day
The speed of blood flow in the renal artery
The volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute
The amount of glucose reabsorbed per minute
questions.x: GFR is the volume of filtrate formed each minute by all the glomeruli of both kidneys, about 120-125 mL per minute in a healthy adult. Urine volume is far smaller because most filtrate is reabsorbed.

questions.q: Young children cannot control urination, but older children and adults can. This voluntary control depends mainly on the:
o: Internal sphincter of smooth muscle at the bladder neck
External urethral sphincter of skeletal muscle
Valves at the ends of the collecting ducts
questions.x: The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control, which a child learns to use. The internal sphincter is smooth muscle and works involuntarily.

questions.q: The kidneys are said to keep the 'internal environment' constant. The internal environment means the:
o: Blood plasma and tissue fluid that bathe the body's cells
questions.x: The internal environment is the fluid surrounding the cells: tissue fluid and plasma. The gut contents, bladder urine and lung air are effectively outside the body tissues.

questions.q: Urine is said to be supersaturated with calcium oxalate when:
o: More calcium oxalate is dissolved than the urine can normally hold, so crystals can form
The urine contains no calcium oxalate at all
All the calcium oxalate is already solid
The urine is more dilute than blood plasma
questions.x: Supersaturation means the salt concentration is above its normal solubility limit, which is the condition that allows crystals and stones to form.

questions.q: A labelled RNA probe for a particular gene's mRNA is applied to a slice of tissue and gives a strong signal. This shows that in that tissue the gene is:
questions.x: The probe binds to mRNA, and mRNA is present only when the gene is being transcribed. All body cells carry the gene, but only cells expressing it contain its mRNA.

questions.q: Which recombinant product is used to PREVENT a disease rather than to treat it?
questions.x: The recombinant hepatitis B vaccine is given to healthy people so they become immune before infection. Insulin, factor VIII and erythropoietin replace substances missing in people who already have a disorder.

questions.q: For prenatal diagnosis of a genetic disorder with DNA probes, fetal cells are usually obtained by:
o: Taking a blood sample from the father
Testing the mother's urine for hCG
Collecting cells from the mother's mouth
questions.x: Amniocentesis collects fetal cells from the amniotic fluid, and chorionic villus sampling takes cells from the developing placenta. Both provide fetal DNA; the father's or mother's own cells do not.

questions.q: The antibiotic penicillin is produced commercially by growing:
o: The fungus Penicillium in large fermenters
questions.x: Penicillin is made by the mould Penicillium, grown in large fermenters under controlled conditions; the antibiotic is then extracted and purified.

questions.q: For 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃, 3 mol of aluminium is heated with 3 mol of chlorine. What is the maximum amount of AlCl₃ formed?
questions.x: 3 mol Al would need 4.5 mol Cl₂, so Cl₂ is limiting. 3 mol Cl₂ × 2/3 = 2 mol AlCl₃. 3 mol assumes aluminium is limiting.

questions.q: Sodium reacts with water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. What volume of hydrogen at STP is given off by 4.6 g of sodium? (Na = 23)
questions.x: Moles of Na = 4.6/23 = 0.2 mol; ratio Na : H₂ = 2 : 1, so 0.1 mol H₂ = 0.1 × 22.4 = 2.24 dm³. 4.48 dm³ ignores the 2 : 1 ratio.

questions.q: The two lobes of a pz orbital lie along the:
o: Line between the x- and y-axes
questions.x: Each p orbital is named after the axis along which its two lobes point, so pz lies along the z-axis.

questions.q: Compared with a 2p orbital, a 3p orbital has:
o: The same dumbbell shape but a larger size and higher energy
A spherical shape and a larger size
The same size but a different orientation only
A dumbbell shape but a smaller size and lower energy
questions.x: All p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped; as n increases from 2 to 3, the orbital becomes larger and higher in energy.

questions.q: The electronic configuration of calcium (Z = 20) is:
questions.x: After argon (18 electrons), the next two go into 4s, which is lower in energy than 3d, giving [Ar] 4s².

questions.q: Graphs of volume against pressure are drawn for the same gas sample at two temperatures, T₁ and T₂, where T₂ is higher than T₁. Compared with the T₁ curve, the T₂ curve:
o: Lies further from the axes, giving a larger volume at each pressure
Lies closer to the axes, giving a smaller volume at each pressure
Is a straight line instead of a curve
questions.x: Each isotherm obeys PV = constant, and the constant is larger at the higher temperature. So at any pressure the volume is larger, and the T₂ curve lies further from the axes.

questions.q: Two gases are in identical flasks at the same pressure, each containing the same number of molecules. From PV = ⅓mNc̄², the gas with heavier molecules must have:
o: Molecules that do not collide with the walls
questions.x: With P, V and N the same, the product mc̄² must be the same for both gases. A larger mass m therefore needs a smaller c̄²: heavier molecules move more slowly.

questions.q: Hydrogen (M = 2) is at 300 K. At what temperature would oxygen (M = 32) have the same root mean square speed? (Use speed = √(3RT/M).)
questions.x: Equal speeds need equal T/M: 300/2 = T/32, so T = 300 × 16 = 4800 K. Using √16 = 4 gives the wrong value 1200 K.

questions.q: When 1.00 dm³ of water (1.00 g cm⁻³) freezes, the ice formed (density 0.92 g cm⁻³) has a volume of about:
questions.x: Mass = 1000 g. Volume of ice = 1000/0.92 ≈ 1087 cm³ ≈ 1.09 dm³, i.e. water expands by about 9% on freezing.

questions.q: Water in an open dish evaporates faster on a windy day because the moving air:
o: Lowers the temperature of the water
Increases the intermolecular forces at the surface
Raises the external pressure on the water
Carries vapour molecules away, so fewer return to the liquid
questions.x: Wind removes vapour from above the surface, so fewer molecules condense back and the net rate of evaporation rises.

questions.q: As the radius ratio of an MX ionic crystal increases from about 0.3 to about 0.8, the coordination number of the cation:
questions.x: A ratio of 0.3 lies in the tetrahedral range (4) and 0.8 lies above 0.732 (8). A larger cation can fit more anions around it.

questions.q: CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g), ΔH negative. The equilibrium yield of methanol is greatest at:
questions.x: 3 mol of gas give 1 mol, so high pressure favours methanol; the forward reaction is exothermic, so low temperature also favours it.

questions.q: At constant temperature, a reaction mixture in a closed vessel has reached equilibrium when its:
o: Reactants have all been used up
Colour, pressure and concentrations no longer change
questions.x: At equilibrium, measurable (macroscopic) properties such as colour, pressure and concentration become constant, though both reactions continue.

questions.q: A metal hydroxide M(OH)₂ has Ksp = 4 × 10⁻¹² at 25 °C. How many moles of it dissolve per dm³ of pure water?
questions.x: If s mol dissolve, [M²⁺] = s and [OH⁻] = 2s, so Ksp = 4s³ = 4 × 10⁻¹². s³ = 1 × 10⁻¹², s = 1 × 10⁻⁴. Treating it as a 1 : 1 salt gives 2 × 10⁻⁶.

questions.q: Which of the following quantities always has a positive value?
questions.x: There is always an energy barrier to climb, so Ea is positive. ΔH, enthalpy of solution and ΔE may be positive or negative.

questions.q: Two reactions have the same pre-exponential factor and are run at the same temperature, but reaction X has a higher Ea than reaction Y. Which is correct?
o: X has the smaller rate constant
X has the larger rate constant
Both have the same rate constant
The rate constants cannot be compared without concentrations
questions.x: From k = A e^(−Ea/RT), with A and T the same, a larger Ea makes the exponential term smaller, so k is smaller. k does not depend on concentration.

questions.q: In the reaction OH⁻ + CH₃Br → CH₃OH + Br⁻ (a one-step substitution), the activated complex is best described as:
o: [HO···CH₃···Br]⁻, with the C–O bond partly formed and the C–Br bond partly broken
CH₃⁺ and Br⁻ completely separated before OH⁻ attacks
CH₃OH and Br⁻ already fully formed
CH₃Br and OH⁻ approaching without any bond change
questions.x: In a one-step substitution, bond making and bond breaking happen together; the activated complex has both bonds partial. A free carbocation belongs to a two-step mechanism.

questions.q: In an energy cycle, X can change into Z directly (ΔH₁), or first into Y (ΔH₂) and then into Z (ΔH₃). According to Hess's law:
questions.x: The enthalpy change from X to Z is the same by either route, so the direct value equals the sum of the steps of the indirect route.

questions.q: Which pair of properties are BOTH state functions?
questions.x: Pressure, temperature, internal energy and enthalpy depend only on the state of the system. Heat and work depend on the path.

questions.q: Silver nitrate solution should not be stored in a copper vessel. Given E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V and E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, the reason is that:
o: Copper reduces Ag⁺ to silver and itself dissolves as Cu²⁺
Silver ions oxidise water and release oxygen
Copper is oxidised by nitrate to give hydrogen gas
Silver metal reduces Cu²⁺ ions to copper
questions.x: Ag⁺/Ag has the higher E°, so Ag⁺ is reduced and copper (lower E°) is oxidised: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag.

questions.q: Which of the following processes involves a redox reaction?
questions.x: In rusting, iron is oxidised by oxygen. The other three are physical changes with no transfer of electrons.

questions.q: The electronegativity of a carbon atom increases with the s character of its hybrid orbitals. Which order of electronegativity is correct?
o: sp³ carbon > sp² carbon > sp carbon
sp carbon > sp² carbon > sp³ carbon
sp² carbon > sp carbon > sp³ carbon
questions.x: s character is 50% in sp, 33% in sp² and 25% in sp³. More s character holds electrons closer to the nucleus, so sp carbon is the most electronegative.

questions.q: Of the three isomeric dichlorobenzenes, which one is non-polar?
questions.x: In 1,4-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl dipoles lie on opposite sides of the flat ring and cancel. In the 1,2 and 1,3 isomers the dipoles are at an angle and do not cancel.

questions.q: A lone pair repels more strongly than a bond pair because a lone pair:
o: Contains more electrons than a bond pair
Lies farther from the central nucleus
Is held by only one nucleus and so spreads out more
questions.x: A lone pair is attracted by only the central nucleus, so its electron cloud is broader and closer to the central atom, pushing bond pairs together. Both lone and bond pairs contain two electrons.

questions.q: On going down Group IV from carbon to lead, the stability of the +4 oxidation state:
o: Increases, while that of the +2 state decreases
Stays the same for all elements
Decreases, while that of the +2 state increases
Decreases, and so does that of the +2 state
questions.x: Because of the inert pair effect, the ns² pair is held more firmly in heavier elements, so +2 becomes more stable than +4 towards lead.

questions.q: The thermal stability of the Group IV hydrides MH₄ changes down the group. Which is the least stable?
questions.x: As the atom gets larger the M–H bond becomes longer and weaker, so stability falls from CH₄ to PbH₄, which hardly exists.

questions.q: Many compounds of transition elements are attracted into a magnetic field (they are paramagnetic). This is due to:
o: Paired electrons in their p orbitals
Unpaired electrons in their d orbitals
questions.x: Paramagnetism comes from unpaired electrons, and transition metal ions often have partly filled d subshells with unpaired electrons. Paired electrons do not cause attraction into a field.

questions.q: Propenoic acid (acrylic acid), CH₂=CHCOOH, contains which functional groups?
o: A carbonyl group and a hydroxyl group of an alcohol
A carbon–carbon double bond and an ester group
A carbon–carbon double bond and a carboxyl group
An aldehyde group and a hydroxyl group
questions.x: CH₂=CH– is an alkene double bond and –COOH is the carboxyl group. Although –COOH contains C=O and –OH, together they form one carboxyl group, not a ketone and alcohol.

questions.q: The measured enthalpy of combustion of benzene is less negative than the value calculated for a cyclohexatriene structure with three localised double bonds. This is evidence that benzene:
o: Is less stable than the Kekulé structure
Contains fewer hydrogen atoms than expected
questions.x: Less heat released means the real molecule started at lower energy than the Kekulé model predicts. The difference is the resonance energy.

questions.q: When bromoethane is heated with alcoholic KOH to give ethene, the other products are:
questions.x: CH₃CH₂Br + KOH → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O. The H and Br removed from the alkyl halide end up as water and potassium bromide.

questions.q: A straight-chain alkyne with five carbons has the structure CH₃C≡CCH₂CH₃. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.x: The chain has five carbons. Numbering from the end nearer the triple bond puts it between C2 and C3, so the name is pent-2-yne, not pent-3-yne.

questions.q: Which of the following species is a free radical?
questions.x: Cl• is a neutral chlorine atom with one unpaired electron. Cl⁻ and Cl⁺ are ions, and Cl₂ is a molecule with all electrons paired.

questions.q: In the electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene, the intermediate formed after the first step is:
questions.x: H⁺ attaches to one carbon of the double bond, leaving a positive charge on the other: CH₃CH₂⁺. Br⁻ then joins this carbocation.

questions.q: An –OH group attached to a benzene ring is:
questions.x: The –OH group donates electron density to the ring, making it more reactive and directing incoming electrophiles to the 2 and 4 positions.

questions.q: 37.6 g of 1,2-dibromoethane (M = 188 g mol⁻¹) is converted completely into ethyne. What mass of ethyne is formed? (C 12, H 1)
questions.x: Moles = 37.6/188 = 0.2. One mole of dibromide gives one mole of C₂H₂ (M = 26), so mass = 0.2 × 26 = 5.2 g.

questions.q: Bromoethane reacts with alcoholic potassium cyanide, KCN. The organic product and the change in the carbon chain are:
o: CH₃CN; chain shorter by one carbon
CH₃CH₂CN; chain longer by one carbon
questions.x: CN⁻ replaces Br⁻, giving propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN. The carbon of the CN group adds one carbon to the chain, which is why this reaction is used to step up a chain.

questions.q: In the transition state of an SN2 reaction of CH₃Br with OH⁻, the central carbon atom is:
o: Fully bonded to OH, with Br already gone
A planar carbocation with no nucleophile attached
Part of a stable carbanion intermediate
Partly bonded to both the OH group and the Br atom
questions.x: In SN2 the C–O bond forms while the C–Br bond breaks, so in the transition state the carbon is partly bonded to both. A carbocation belongs to SN1, and SN2 has no intermediate.

questions.q: Sec-butyl alcohol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃, should be named by IUPAC rules as:
questions.x: The longest chain has four carbons and is numbered from the end nearer the –OH, putting it on C-2. 'Butan-3-ol' numbers from the wrong end.

questions.q: In the Williamson synthesis of ethers, an alkyl halide is treated with sodium alkoxide. The alkoxide ion acts as:
o: An electrophile that attacks the halogen
A nucleophile that replaces the halogen
A dehydrating agent that removes water
questions.x: The alkoxide ion, RO⁻, has a negative oxygen with lone pairs, so it attacks the carbon of the alkyl halide and displaces the halide ion in a nucleophilic substitution, giving R–O–R′.

questions.q: The cyanohydrin obtained from acetone (propanone) has the formula:
questions.x: H adds to the oxygen and CN to the carbonyl carbon: (CH₃)₂C=O + HCN → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN, 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile. CH₃CH(OH)CN is the cyanohydrin of ethanal.

questions.q: A carbonyl compound X, C₅H₁₀O, is reduced by NaBH₄ to pentan-3-ol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. X is:
questions.x: Reduction turns C=O into CH–OH at the same position, so the –OH on C-3 must come from a C=O on C-3: CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃, pentan-3-one. Pentanal would give pentan-1-ol.

questions.q: Ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂, is boiled with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The products are:
questions.x: Alkaline hydrolysis of an amide gives the carboxylate salt and ammonia gas: CH₃CONH₂ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + NH₃.

questions.q: At a fixed enzyme concentration, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction is measured at increasing substrate concentrations. The rate rises and then levels off because:
o: The enzyme is denatured at high substrate concentration
The activation energy rises as more substrate is added
The products react back to form the substrate
All the active sites become occupied, so the enzyme is saturated
questions.x: At low substrate concentration more substrate means more enzyme–substrate complexes. Once every active site is busy, adding substrate cannot raise the rate further.

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT denature a protein?
o: Dissolving it in water at room temperature
Adding salts of heavy metals such as Hg²⁺
questions.x: Heat, strong acids and heavy-metal ions disrupt the bonds that hold the folded shape. Simply dissolving a soluble protein in water at room temperature leaves its structure intact.

questions.q: Which property is typical of a thermoplastic adhesive?
o: It sets by forming a permanent cross-linked network
It softens each time it is heated and hardens again on cooling
It needs a hardener mixed in just before use
It sets only when it absorbs moisture
questions.x: Thermoplastic adhesives have chains that are not cross-linked, so they melt and reset repeatedly. A permanent cross-linked network and a hardener are features of thermosetting adhesives.

questions.q: Two vectors keep their magnitudes but the angle between them is varied. Their cross product has its largest magnitude at an angle of:
questions.x: |P × Q| = PQ sin θ, and sin θ has its largest value of 1 at θ = 90°. At 0° and 180° it is zero.

questions.q: A stone thrown horizontally from a roof moves in two dimensions because it:
o: Keeps its horizontal velocity while gaining vertical velocity due to gravity
Has acceleration in both the horizontal and vertical directions
Loses horizontal velocity as it falls
Moves only under its horizontal velocity
questions.x: Gravity acts only vertically, so the stone keeps its horizontal velocity and also gains downward velocity. The two motions together give a curved, two-dimensional path.

questions.q: Over 3 s of flight, by how much does a projectile's vertical velocity change? (g = 10 m s⁻², air drag negligible)
questions.x: The vertical acceleration is 10 m s⁻² downward, so in 3 s the vertical velocity changes by 10 × 3 = 30 m s⁻¹ downward. 45 is the vertical distance a body would fall from rest, not the velocity change.

questions.q: Find the greatest height reached by a ball launched at 20 m s⁻¹, 60° to the horizontal. (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 60° = √3/2, no air drag)
questions.x: H = v² sin²θ / 2g = 400 × (3/4) ÷ 20 = 15 m. 20 m would be the height if it were thrown straight up.

questions.q: The horizontal range of a projectile equals its horizontal velocity multiplied by its time of flight. The time of flight is decided by:
questions.x: The projectile lands when its vertical displacement returns to zero, which depends only on the vertical component of velocity and g. The horizontal motion then gives the range.

questions.q: The launch angle of a projectile on level ground is raised from 45° to 60°, keeping the same speed. Ignoring air resistance, its range and maximum height:
questions.x: Range ∝ sin 2θ, which is greatest at 45°, so the range falls. Maximum height ∝ sin²θ, which keeps rising with θ, so the height increases.

questions.q: Which one of these moves as a projectile?
o: A lift moving up its shaft
A javelin after it leaves the athlete's hand
The blade of a rotating ceiling fan
A car moving along a straight road
questions.x: Once released, the javelin moves forward and falls under gravity at the same time, following a curved path in a vertical plane: projectile motion.

questions.q: A 1 kg stone rests at the bottom of a well 10 m deep. Taking ground level as zero, the potential energy of the stone is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
questions.x: The stone is 10 m below the reference level: PE = 1 × 10 × (−10) = −100 J. −10 J forgets to multiply by g.

questions.q: A 6 kg block is pulled 4 m up a smooth incline that makes 30° with the horizontal, at constant speed, by a force parallel to the incline. The work done by this force is (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 30° = 0.5):
questions.x: At constant speed on a smooth incline the pull equals mg sin 30° = 60 × 0.5 = 30 N. W = 30 × 4 = 120 J. Using mg × 4 = 240 J forgets the sine factor.

questions.q: An angle of π/3 rad expressed in degrees is:
A wheel rotates clockwise as seen by an observer facing it. By the right-hand rule, its angular velocity points:
o: Along the axle, towards the observer
Along the tangent to the rim
Along the axle, away from the observer
questions.x: Curl the right-hand fingers clockwise (as seen); the thumb points away from the observer along the axle. Angular velocity is always along the axis.

questions.q: What speed must a bead of radius 2 × 10⁻³ m have for the viscous force F = 6πηrv acting on it to be 6π × 10⁻⁴ N, when η = 0.5 Pa s?
As a car speeds up from a very low speed to a high speed, the air flow around it changes from:
o: Mainly laminar to turbulent, with eddies forming behind the car
questions.x: At low speed air flows smoothly round the car; above the critical speed the flow becomes turbulent, with eddies forming in the wake behind it.

questions.q: Thick honey poured slowly from a jar does NOT behave as an ideal fluid mainly because:
questions.x: An ideal fluid is non-viscous. Honey has large internal friction (viscosity); it is nearly incompressible, and slow honey flow is laminar, not turbulent.

questions.q: A wave travels along a light rope that is joined to a much heavier rope. As the wave passes into the heavier rope, which quantity stays the same?
questions.x: The frequency is set by the source and cannot change at the join. The speed is smaller in the heavier rope, so the wavelength changes too.

questions.q: Light waves are:
questions.x: Light consists of electric and magnetic fields vibrating perpendicular to the direction of travel, so it is a transverse electromagnetic wave. It can be polarised, which confirms this.

questions.q: A small folded paper rider is placed on a stretched wire vibrating in a stationary wave. The rider is thrown off when it is placed at:
questions.x: The rider is thrown off where the wire vibrates with the greatest amplitude, at an antinode. At a node (including the fixed ends) the wire does not move, so the rider stays.

questions.q: A student moves one end of a long rope up and down 4 times per second. A crest is seen to travel 6 m along the rope in 2 s. The wavelength of the waves on the rope is:
questions.x: Speed v = 6/2 = 3 m s⁻¹ and f = 4 Hz, so λ = v/f = 3/4 = 0.75 m. Dividing 6 m by 4 (1.5 m) forgets that the crest took 2 s.

questions.q: A particle of a medium completes 120 vibrations in one minute as a wave passes. The time period of the wave is:
questions.x: Frequency = 120/60 = 2 Hz, so T = 1/f = 0.5 s. Using 120 vibrations per second by mistake gives 0.0083 s.

questions.q: Two waves of the same frequency but amplitudes 3 mm and 2 mm travel in opposite directions along a string. The resulting standing wave pattern has:
o: Maximum amplitude 5 mm and minimum amplitude 1 mm
Maximum amplitude 5 mm and minimum amplitude zero
Maximum amplitude 6 mm and minimum amplitude zero
Maximum amplitude 3 mm and minimum amplitude 2 mm
questions.x: Where the waves always meet in phase the amplitude is 3 + 2 = 5 mm; where they always meet in opposite phase it is 3 − 2 = 1 mm. True nodes of zero amplitude need equal amplitudes.

questions.q: The relation Cp − Cv = R shows that the molar gas constant R has the same unit as:
questions.x: R is the difference of two molar specific heats, so it is measured in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the unit of molar specific heat.

questions.q: In an adiabatic process no heat enters or leaves the gas. With W as the work done by the gas, the first law becomes:
questions.x: Putting Q = 0 into Q = ΔU + W gives ΔU = −W: if the gas does work, its internal energy falls by the same amount.

questions.q: A refrigerator moves thermal energy from its cold inside to the warmer kitchen. It needs electrical energy to do this because:
o: Heat does not flow on its own from a colder body to a hotter one
Heat always flows from a smaller body to a larger one
The kitchen has less internal energy than the inside
Cold flows out of the refrigerator into the kitchen
questions.x: Left alone, thermal energy flows only from higher to lower temperature. Moving it the other way needs work to be done, which the compressor supplies.

questions.q: Two large thin parallel sheets each carry the SAME positive surface charge density +σ. Each sheet alone produces a field σ/2ε₀. The field in the space between them and outside them is:
questions.x: Between the sheets the two fields point in opposite directions and cancel. Outside, both point away from the sheets in the same direction and add to σ/ε₀. This is the reverse of oppositely charged plates.

questions.q: In a field-line diagram, the number of lines drawn starting or ending on a point charge is chosen to be proportional to:
questions.x: A larger charge produces a stronger field, shown by more lines. Drawing lines in proportion to the charge keeps the line density a fair measure of field strength.

questions.q: The separation of two point charges is cut to half and, at the same time, the space around them is filled with an insulator of εr = 2. If the original force in vacuum was F, it is now:
questions.x: Halving r multiplies the force by 4; the medium divides it by 2. So the new force is 4F/2 = 2F.

questions.q: Electric current has a direction, yet it is treated as a scalar quantity because:
o: Currents add by ordinary arithmetic, not by the laws of vector addition
It always flows in a straight line
Its direction is always from negative to positive
questions.x: Currents meeting at a junction simply add as numbers, whatever the angles between the wires, so current does not obey vector addition and is a scalar.

questions.q: A cell of internal resistance 2 Ω delivers a current of 0.5 A to an external circuit. The 'lost volts' inside the cell are:
questions.x: Lost volts = Ir = 0.5 × 2 = 1 V, the difference between the emf and the terminal potential difference.

questions.q: A neutron moves at high speed at right angles to a strong uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on it is:
o: Maximum, because it moves at 90° to the field
Zero, because it has no charge
Along its velocity, speeding it up
Opposite to its velocity, slowing it down
questions.x: F = qvB sin θ and a neutron has q = 0, so it feels no magnetic force and moves straight on.

questions.q: A power of 100 kW is transmitted at 10 kV through cables of total resistance 5 Ω. The power lost as heat in the cables is:
Electrical power is distributed as AC rather than DC mainly because AC:
o: Has no heating effect in the cables
Can be stepped up and down easily with transformers
Needs no return path to complete the circuit
questions.x: Transformers only work with changing current, so AC voltage can be raised for transmission and lowered for use. AC still heats cables.

questions.q: A 110 Ω resistor is connected to a 220 V (rms) AC supply. The rms current through it is:
questions.x: For a resistor, Ohm's law applies to rms values: I = V/R = 220/110 = 2 A, in phase with the voltage.

questions.q: Ultraviolet radiation of wavelength 200 nm shines on a surface that needs 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J to free an electron. With what largest kinetic energy do electrons emerge? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
Compared with the photon from the n = 3 → n = 2 transition in hydrogen, the photon from the n = 4 → n = 2 transition has:
o: The same energy, since both end on n = 2
questions.x: The drop from n = 4 is larger than from n = 3, so the photon has more energy; since E = hc/λ, its wavelength is shorter.

questions.q: In the simple nuclear model, the diameter of an atom compared with that of its nucleus is:
questions.x: An atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ m across and a nucleus about 10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻¹⁴ m, so the atom is roughly 10⁴ to 10⁵ times larger; it is mostly empty space.

questions.q: The SI unit of equivalent dose, which allows for the different biological effects of different radiations, is the:
questions.x: Equivalent dose is measured in sieverts (Sv). The gray measures absorbed energy per kilogram, and the becquerel and curie measure activity.

questions.q: "The traffic police officer was fined for parking his car in a no-parking zone." This sentence is an example of:
questions.x: It is irony because the result is the opposite of what we expect: the man who enforces parking rules breaks one himself. There is no comparison or exaggeration.

questions.q: Sara reported a question she was asked. Which version is punctuated correctly?
o: Sara asked me where I lived.
Sara asked me where I lived?
Sara asked me, where I lived?
questions.x: An indirect question is a statement, so it ends with a full stop and needs no question mark or quotation marks.

questions.q: Choose the correct option: "Only after the doctor arrived ___ calm down."
questions.x: 'Only after ...' at the start causes inversion in the main clause: 'did' + subject + base verb.

questions.q: What kind of sentence is "How fast that horse runs!"?
questions.x: It expresses strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark, so it is exclamatory, even though it begins with 'How'.

questions.q: In "I will wait here until you return", the words 'until you return' form:
questions.x: They contain a subject and verb and tell when the waiting will end, so they form an adverb clause of time.

questions.q: In "Fatima sang the national anthem sweetly", the word 'sweetly' is an adverb of:
questions.x: Adverbs of manner tell how something is done; 'sweetly' tells how she sang.

questions.q: Report in indirect speech: Hamza said to me, "Can you help me with this sum?"
o: Hamza asked me if I can help him with this sum.
Hamza said to me could I help him with that sum.
Hamza asked me if I could help him with that sum.
Hamza asked me that could I help him with that sum.
questions.x: A yes/no question is reported with 'asked + if', 'can' becomes 'could', and 'this' becomes 'that'.

questions.q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "She did not knew the answer to the last question."
o: She did not known the answer to the last question.
She does not knew the answer to the last question.
She did not knowing the answer to the last question.
She did not know the answer to the last question.
questions.x: After the helping verb 'did', the main verb takes its base form: 'did not know'. The past tense is already shown by 'did'.

questions.q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "To get a good score, regular practice must be done."
o: To get a good score, regular practice must be done by it.
To get a good score, regular practice is must.
To get a good score, you must practise regularly.
To getting a good score, you must practise regularly.
questions.x: The opening phrase 'To get a good score' needs a person as the subject who does the getting; 'regular practice' cannot get a score. Adding 'you' as subject removes the dangling modifier.

questions.q: Statement: Should every college have a staff member trained in first aid? Argument I: Yes, injuries and fainting can happen at any time, and quick first aid can prevent harm. Argument II: No, every city already has a hospital. Which argument is strong?
o: Both arguments I and II are strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
questions.x: Argument I gives a practical reason about help in the first minutes. Argument II is weak because a hospital may be far away when help is needed at once.

questions.q: Find the next number: 1, 10, 3, 20, 5, 30, ?
questions.x: Two series are mixed: 1, 3, 5 (add 2) and 10, 20, 30 (add 10). The seventh term belongs to the first series, so it is 7.

questions.q: Find the next number: 720, 360, 120, 30, 6, ?
questions.x: The terms are divided by 2, 3, 4 and 5 in turn. The next divisor is 6, so 6 / 6 = 1.

questions.q: Faisal is taller than Usman. Usman is taller than Zain. Asad is shorter than Zain. Kashif is shorter than Usman but taller than Zain. Who is in the middle when the five stand in order of height?
questions.x: From tallest: Faisal, Usman, Kashif, Zain, Asad. The third of five is Kashif.

questions.q: In a code language, "tak lo mi" means "clean your room", "mi sar pe" means "room is big" and "pe dun tak" means "big clean house". What is the code for "house"?
questions.x: 'mi' is common to the first two (room), 'pe' to the last two (big) and 'tak' to the first and third (clean). The remaining word in the third phrase, 'dun', means house.

questions.q: Statement: Shops in a market keep catching fire because of overloaded electric connections. Courses of action: I. The wiring should be inspected and overloaded connections fixed. II. Fire extinguishers should be placed in the market. III. Electricity to the market should be cut off permanently. Which course(s) of action follow?
o: I, II and III all follow
questions.x: Fixing the wiring prevents fires and extinguishers limit damage if one starts. Cutting power for good would shut down the market, so III is extreme.

questions.q: Statement: A fire broke out in a cloth market because of faulty electric wiring in one shop. Courses of action: I. The electric wiring of the shops in the market should be inspected. II. All cloth markets in the country should be closed. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Inspecting the wiring deals with the stated cause of the fire. Closing every cloth market in the country is extreme and does not follow from one fire.

questions.q: Hira says her plant grew faster this month because she talked kindly to it every morning. During the same month, she had moved it to a much sunnier window. Which is the most valid conclusion?
o: Talking to the plant must be the only reason for its growth
The plant would have died if she had stopped talking
The move to more sunlight is a known cause of faster growth and could explain the change
Plants grow faster only when people are near them
questions.x: Plants need light to make food, so more sunlight can explain faster growth. Because two things changed at once, the talking cannot be proved to be the cause.

questions.q: People in a village believe that eating fish and then drinking milk causes white patches on the skin. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: Fish and milk are both expensive
Milk is drunk mostly at breakfast
Many people in the village believe it
White patches result from loss of the skin's pigment cells, and no study has linked them to eating fish with milk
questions.x: The patches are due to loss of pigment-making cells in the skin. With no evidence of any link to the food, the belief should be rejected.
